scope: Fuzzing, observability, telemetry, durable workflows and streaming data systems
method: Pinned official repository README and license/source-path inspection with upstream HEAD revisions recorded. Findings are bounded research notes; no REA execution, package installation, SYLPH code patch, build, or runtime test was performed.

provenance: Official README and license files inspected at pinned commit bf2fc668dafda5295aa6fd01825ee67b885f0f2b (main); accessed 2026-10-14.
discoveries: cargo-fuzz is a Cargo subcommand for libFuzzer fuzz targets and supports corpus minimization and coverage.
The README requires nightly Rust and LLVM sanitizer support and states native Windows is unsupported.
patterns: Fuzz binary parsers and protocol adapters at isolated Rust boundaries.
Preserve minimized crashing inputs as permanent regression fixtures.
overlap: Fuzzing strategy is useful; cargo-fuzz does not exercise the current TypeScript implementation.
risks: Host platform and toolchain constraints are significant.
This Rust tool does not fuzz the current TypeScript implementation.
validation: Use the existing TypeScript runtime to test equivalent malformed inputs.
If Rust code is added, run on supported Unix CI and retain corpus/seed artifacts.
evidence: Official README and license files inspected at pinned commit bf2fc668dafda5295aa6fd01825ee67b885f0f2b (main); accessed 2026-10-14.

provenance: Official README and repository license metadata inspected at pinned commit 5fcd99aa6dea4bc139097527901f6c25a52baca5 (main); accessed 2026-10-14.
discoveries: Loki is a log storage/query service using multidimensional labels and push-based log delivery.
The current README identifies Grafana Alloy as the collection agent and says Promtail is feature complete.
Loki can add operational log search but does not provide canonical evidence or execution truth.
patterns: Use bounded-cardinality labels such as service, environment, and component.
Keep wallet secrets, raw keys, and high-volume transaction payloads out of logs; correlate by safe request/event IDs.
overlap: Would complement application logs; current registry does not establish a Loki deployment.
risks: High-cardinality labels increase storage/query cost.
The repository is AGPL-3.0; deployment and licensing requirements need review.
Logs must not become a mutable source of truth for fills or feed readiness.
validation: Prototype with synthetic logs only.
Verify redaction, retention, access controls, and label cardinality before any deployment.
evidence: Official README and repository license metadata inspected at pinned commit 5fcd99aa6dea4bc139097527901f6c25a52baca5 (main); accessed 2026-10-14.

provenance: Official README and LICENSING.md references inspected at pinned commit c478488929811c041227991f1b0601864dab7c8c (main); accessed 2026-10-14.
discoveries: Tempo is a high-volume distributed tracing backend compatible with Jaeger, Zipkin, Kafka, and OpenTelemetry formats.
Trace receiver/wire/storage formats build on OpenTelemetry standards and can store to object storage or local disk.
Tempo repository license is AGPL-3.0-only with separately documented Apache-2.0 exceptions.
patterns: Propagate safe correlation IDs across ingress, recovery, projection, and dashboard requests.
Record provider, slot, queue-depth, and phase timing as bounded span attributes; avoid secrets and raw wallet data.
overlap: Tracing can make existing boundaries observable without adding a second state authority.
risks: Unbounded trace attributes can expose sensitive values and create storage cost.
A tracing backend is observational only and cannot certify state correctness.
License exceptions require file/component-level review.
validation: Use synthetic requests to verify trace continuity and redaction.
Measure sampling, retention, and loss behavior; separately compare traces with journal evidence.
evidence: Official README and LICENSING.md references inspected at pinned commit c478488929811c041227991f1b0601864dab7c8c (main); accessed 2026-10-14.
sources.license: AGPL-3.0-only; Apache-2.0 exceptions documented in LICENSING.md

provenance: Official README and license section inspected at pinned commit 3e09090df7bab6a01016d54bb359e16a4fa3648c (master); accessed 2026-10-14.
discoveries: k6 is a Go-based load-testing tool with an embedded JavaScript API and HTTP, WebSocket, gRPC, browser, and other protocol support.
Tests as code can define staged workloads and thresholds such as percentile response-time objectives.
The repository is AGPL-3.0; using the CLI as a test tool does not mean it should be embedded into the Engine.
patterns: Load-test local ingestion mocks and read-only dashboard endpoints using explicit thresholds.
Simulate bursts, reconnects, and slow consumers without sending trades.
overlap: External test tooling; no runtime integration required.
risks: Load against real providers can incur costs or trigger rate limits.
A load test against mocks does not establish production provider throughput.
AGPL-3.0 licensing needs review for any distributed service integration.
validation: Target local or explicitly authorized staging endpoints only.
Record script, threshold, environment, and results; verify request bodies cannot invoke live signing or broadcast.
evidence: Official README and license section inspected at pinned commit 3e09090df7bab6a01016d54bb359e16a4fa3648c (master); accessed 2026-10-14.

provenance: Official README and repository license metadata inspected at pinned commit 9fd22405bb330c6c600d0d2e5ed4806102516636 (main); accessed 2026-10-14.
discoveries: Pyroscope is a continuous profiling platform for CPU, memory, and I/O bottleneck analysis.
Its current 2.0 architecture writes profiles to object storage; SDKs, Alloy, and OTLP/eBPF are described as ingestion options.
Profiling can help isolate event-lane latency regressions but is not itself a monitoring or safety authority.
patterns: Profile local/staging parsers, projection commits, and backfills under representative synthetic load.
Compare profiles across revisions and redact or avoid sensitive labels.
overlap: Observability aid only; does not change ingestion decisions.
risks: Profiles may expose identifiers or application values depending on instrumentation.
A server deployment adds storage/operational complexity; AGPL-3.0 terms and exceptions require review.
validation: Use synthetic data and verify redaction.
Compare CPU/memory profiles with measured throughput, queue growth, and event loss counters.
evidence: Official README and repository license metadata inspected at pinned commit 9fd22405bb330c6c600d0d2e5ed4806102516636 (main); accessed 2026-10-14.

provenance: Official README and repository license metadata inspected at pinned commit 5dba56afa5e0def9745c042de0b996274a430d0c (main); accessed 2026-10-14.
discoveries: Grafana Alloy is an OpenTelemetry Collector distribution with programmable pipelines and built-in Prometheus components.
The README lists metrics, logs, traces, and profiles and integration components for Prometheus, Loki, and Pyroscope.
Alloy is a telemetry collection/processing layer, not an application-state or feed-health authority.
patterns: Use an external collector boundary for telemetry transport and redaction.
Keep the engine’s canonical status and readiness predicates inside SYLPH; export only bounded low-cardinality observations.
overlap: Collector can route existing signals; it should not become a source of trading state.
risks: Pipeline transformations may drop or alter telemetry; collectors are not a canonical evidence journal.
Adding a separate collector deployment increases operational and configuration surface.
validation: Use synthetic telemetry to validate routing, backpressure, and redaction.
Compare exported counters with Engine snapshots without using collector availability to declare feed health.
evidence: Official README and repository license metadata inspected at pinned commit 5dba56afa5e0def9745c042de0b996274a430d0c (main); accessed 2026-10-14.

provenance: Official repository README and Apache-2.0 license metadata inspected at pinned commit 6e69e843b38d22ded60a13e0163f6326136f59fa (main); accessed 2026-10-14.
discoveries: Prometheus is a monitoring system and time-series database with its own scrape, query, and alerting workflows.
The repository supports configurable service-discovery plugins and build/test/vet commands.
Prometheus metrics can characterize queue depth, event throughput, reconnects, and commit latency but do not prove persisted journal state.
patterns: Expose bounded-cardinality counters and histograms for admitted/rejected events, queue depth, projection latency, reconnects, and gap detection.
Keep dimensions bounded; use slot/tx IDs in traces or logs rather than metric labels.
overlap: Metrics export complements current state snapshots; no need to embed Prometheus into the engine.
risks: High-cardinality labels can overwhelm time-series storage.
Metrics are sampled/observational and may be delayed or unavailable; do not make readiness depend solely on them.
validation: Compare metrics with deterministic event/journal counts and restart recovery.
Test stale scrape and collector failure without changing the Engine’s fail-closed readiness.
evidence: Official repository README and Apache-2.0 license metadata inspected at pinned commit 6e69e843b38d22ded60a13e0163f6326136f59fa (main); accessed 2026-10-14.

provenance: Official README and repository license metadata inspected at pinned commit 46a0454806fd024159597fe651a16defb666e672 (main); accessed 2026-10-14.
discoveries: OpenTelemetry Collector source is organized around receivers, processors, exporters, pipelines, and service configuration.
The upstream project documents signed container image verification using Sigstore Cosign.
Collector pipelines transport and transform telemetry; they are distinct from source-of-truth trade/recovery state.
patterns: Use a small, explicitly configured telemetry pipeline and verify component compatibility.
Verify signed release images and pin distribution/version when deploying.
overlap: Could export engine metrics/traces without coupling the engine to a backend.
risks: Unverified or excessive components expand supply-chain and operational risk.
Processor configuration can alter/drop data; telemetry delivery is not equivalent to durable canonical journaling.
validation: Test collector configs with synthetic data and assert expected redaction/outputs.
Verify image signatures and pinned versions; inject exporter outage and inspect loss/retry behavior.
evidence: Official README and repository license metadata inspected at pinned commit 46a0454806fd024159597fe651a16defb666e672 (main); accessed 2026-10-14.

provenance: Official README and MIT license inspected at pinned commit 1872297dceb4f82309ef3ba0922c688212417e34 (main); accessed 2026-10-14.
discoveries: Temporal server durably executes application Workflows and automatically handles intermittent failures and retries.
The server repository is distinct from the language SDKs used to author Workflows, Activities, and Workers.
Workflow retries can replay Activities; side effects therefore require idempotency and an explicit activity boundary.
patterns: For long-running historical backfills, model idempotent work units, durable checkpoints, and explicit retry policy.
Keep recovery orchestration separate from live trading workflows and signing authority.
overlap: Existing gap reconciler and checkpointing already own recovery semantics; Temporal is not justified without a concrete orchestration gap.
risks: Retries can duplicate side effects unless activities are idempotent.
A distributed workflow engine expands operational complexity and can cause unexpected external calls if not strictly scoped.
validation: Prototype against a local test server with idempotent test-only activities.
Prove retries cannot invoke signing, broadcast, or capital-moving paths.
evidence: Official README and MIT license inspected at pinned commit 1872297dceb4f82309ef3ba0922c688212417e34 (main); accessed 2026-10-14.

provenance: Official repository README and Apache-2.0 license metadata inspected at pinned commit 64dda80fdd87b41b2afcdc5faf5d846db6c189b0 (main); accessed 2026-10-14.
discoveries: NATS Server is a messaging system supporting publish/subscribe and request/reply patterns.
Durability and replay behavior depend on selected/configured NATS capabilities and deployment, not just a subject subscription.
Broker transport would be an internal distribution layer and must not replace SYLPH canonical ingress receipts.
patterns: Use stable message IDs, explicit acknowledgements, replay-safe consumers, and preserve source slot/intent metadata.
Keep broker consumers idempotent and separate analytics events from execution-control messages.
overlap: Potential transport pattern only; current ingress path remains source of truth.
risks: At-most-once and at-least-once paths differ and can create gaps or duplicates.
Broker persistence, retention, and availability become operational dependencies.
validation: Inject disconnect, duplicate, out-of-order, and restart scenarios in an isolated harness.
Verify idempotency, offset/checkpoint recovery, and no path to signing or broadcast.
evidence: Official repository README and Apache-2.0 license metadata inspected at pinned commit 64dda80fdd87b41b2afcdc5faf5d846db6c189b0 (main); accessed 2026-10-14.

provenance: Official repository README and root-license path checked against pinned default-branch commit 4254992f6115e92c1dbd86f90bb0aee0b869f15e; accessed 2026-10-15. The root LICENSE path returned 404, so repository-wide licensing was not inferred.
discoveries: Redpanda describes itself as a Kafka-compatible streaming data platform with connectors and configurable tiered storage.
Kafka API compatibility is a product-level description, not proof that every Kafka semantic, ordering, or recovery behavior matches SYLPH requirements.
The inspected repository root did not expose a LICENSE file; licensing of source components remains unresolved from this inspection.
patterns: Consider broker-backed append/replay only for a separately operated analytics or backfill pipeline.
Carry immutable event IDs, processing intent, source slot, and consumer checkpoint in any event envelope.
overlap: A broker could support downstream analytics but would duplicate canonical ingress if inserted in the Engine path.
risks: Kafka API compatibility does not establish exactly-once delivery, source ordering, or replay completeness for a particular configuration.
No root license was found at the pinned revision; source and dependency license obligations need per-component verification before reuse or deployment.
An external broker would add an operational dependency and a second checkpoint/retention boundary.
validation: If evaluated, test duplicates, out-of-order delivery, retention expiry, checkpoint recovery, and consumer replays against an immutable reference ledger.
Keep broker consumers downstream of canonical ingress and outside signing or entry authorization.
sources.license: Root LICENSE not present at pinned revision; component licensing unresolved

provenance: Official RisingWave README and repository license metadata inspected at pinned default-branch commit 1d1c04166fda93756acb1454450d44d69f4434c6; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: RisingWave presents an event-streaming platform that ingests from databases, brokers, webhooks, and historical sources.
Its continuously maintained materialized views are served through SQL, creating an analytical serving layer rather than canonical chain evidence.
The repository advertises Apache-2.0 licensing.
patterns: Model event time and processing time separately, with explicit handling for late and duplicate observations.
Compare incremental aggregates with deterministic batch recomputation.
overlap: Could derive analytics from a downstream normalized event stream; it is not required to repair the in-process feed queue or canonical journal.
risks: Incremental results depend on source ordering, watermark, retention, and recovery semantics that need configuration-level validation.
A derived view must not be treated as authoritative feed health, position, or fill state.
validation: Replay duplicates, late events, restart, and source recovery using deterministic fixtures; compare with a reference batch calculation.
Keep any prototype read-only and downstream of canonical event persistence.

provenance: Official Materialize README and license statement inspected at pinned default-branch commit 1f24515fd7955dc2fb0840b40fedc300fe712c50; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: Materialize incrementally maintains SQL views over changing upstream data and supports PostgreSQL protocol reads plus streaming subscriptions.
The README describes query offload, integration-hub, and operational-data-mesh patterns; these are external serving architectures, not drop-in SYLPH libraries.
The standalone database engine is under BSL 1.1 and converts to Apache-2.0 after four years; its README says single-node use is free forever.
patterns: Use derived SQL views for read-only dashboards and analysis while preserving the canonical journal as the source of truth.
Document data freshness and source version for materialized results.
overlap: Potential external read/query layer over persisted events; overlaps with existing projections and would add a separate service.
risks: BSL 1.1 terms are not equivalent to Apache-2.0 before the stated conversion date; deployment/use rights need review.
Materialized consistency guarantees do not certify source completeness, live feed health, or trading readiness.
Additional service, schema, and upstream lag create another operational boundary.
validation: Verify license against the exact intended use and revision before deployment.
Compare incremental outputs against deterministic recomputation through restart, duplicate, late-event, and correction scenarios.
sources.license: BSL-1.1; README states conversion to Apache-2.0 after four years; single-node use stated free forever

provenance: Official TimescaleDB README, LICENSE, and LICENSE-APACHE inspected at pinned default-branch commit cc75200f4f106615d3f8ee65fcd931334b9db120; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: TimescaleDB is a PostgreSQL extension for time-series and event analytics, including hypertables and columnar storage.
The root LICENSE says source is variously Apache-2.0, Apache-compatible, or Timescale License; it identifies the tsl directory as Timescale-licensed unless a file says otherwise.
The README presents a local quick start for development/testing and points production deployments to separate installation guidance.
patterns: For audit analytics, store source IDs, event timestamps, and immutable record identity; make retention policy distinct from canonical evidence retention.
Benchmark time-partitioned queries using representative event volumes before adopting a separate database.
overlap: Could support analytics, but adds a database and does not replace the current Engine persistence or accounting reconciliation.
risks: License obligations differ by directory and produced shared object; repository-level Apache metadata alone is incomplete.
Database migrations, retention, and backup restoration affect audit completeness.
The README explicitly limits its one-line local installer to development and testing.
validation: Review file/component and binary licensing for the exact deployed feature set.
Test migrations, backup/restore, duplicate handling, UTC boundaries, and reconciliation against canonical fills and fees.
sources.license: Mixed: Apache-2.0 outside tsl by default; Timescale License in tsl unless file overrides; verify exact components

provenance: Official InfluxDB README and license files inspected at pinned main-branch commit 06200ef96ba82c5f6727e5038a83af8e722c6875; accessed 2026-10-15.
discoveries: The current main branch documents InfluxDB 3 Core, using Arrow, DataFusion, and Parquet for event/time-series analytics.
The README lists line-protocol writes and SQL, InfluxQL, and Flight SQL query paths, and distinguishes v3 main from v2 and v1 branches.
The README states the open-source code is offered under MIT or Apache-2.0 at the user’s choice.
patterns: Pin the server generation, write protocol, and query API in any analytics integration contract.
Use time-series storage for operational telemetry or research queries, with bounded labels and explicit retention.
overlap: Potential external observability/analytics store only; it is not canonical fill, paper recovery, or Engine health evidence.
risks: API and query semantics differ across major version branches.
Fast query/ingest claims require workload-specific benchmarking and do not imply durable trading-accounting guarantees.
Adding a second store expands backup, authorization, and retention obligations.
validation: Test write/query precision, restart, retention, and export/reconciliation against a deterministic fixture dataset.
Never use its dashboard values as authoritative execution or health state without reconciliation to canonical records.
sources.license: MIT OR Apache-2.0 (README states user’s choice; both license files present)
